frameworks.name: Three Legs of the Investment Stool
frameworks.definition: Investment capital allocation across three scalable dimensions: money (capital), time/work (team building), and brand/distribution (limited in how many associations it can sustain before losing potency).

frameworks.name: Consulting Background to Small Business Bridge
frameworks.definition: Marrying big business strategy with small business tactics by hiring former big-firm consultants (Bain, McKinsey-type) who want to apply complex problem-solving to scaled small businesses.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi prefers to invest capital and work (team/time) over brand distribution, because brand is limited in how many disparate associations it can sustain before losing potency; while money is highly scalable and associating with too many unrelated things dilutes brand effectiveness.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when building portfolio companies across multiple domains
claims.mechanism: Brand is built on associations; pairing with too many disparate things dilutes potency, while capital deployment and team-building scale without the same constraint.
bounded_by: Associations within similar buckets can maintain more potency than associations across disparate domains

claims.text: At ACQ Ventures, Hormozi hires former big-firm consultants (Bain, McKinsey alumni) who dislike the role-as-a-cog structure of billable-hour consulting but bring exceptional problem-solving capability; these hires combine large-enterprise strategy thinking with small-business execution tactics.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: in advisory/holding company roles at scale
claims.mechanism: Large-firm consultants have practiced problem-solving at enterprise complexity; applying this to smaller-business problems creates a unique capability gap they fill by bridging strategy and execution.
bounded_by: This works specifically for ex-consultants seeking purpose beyond billable hours; not applicable to consultants content with traditional firm role

claims.text: Large-firm consulting analysis (e.g., supply chain optimization for Walmart Brazil) is "really valuable to a big business which is why they pay the money for it" but "not useful at all to a small business"; yet the problem-solving discipline transfers directly to advisory work for scaled small businesses.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when evaluating consulting skill transfer to small business advising
claims.mechanism: Consultants are engineers at core—skilled at solving problems regardless of domain. The thinking process, not the specific domain knowledge, is the transferable asset.

claims.text: Hormozi would not invest in seed-stage content creator businesses with traditional structure (creator majority ownership, investor minority) because creators are typically strong on idea generation but weak on execution and business acumen, and the deal structure carries high risk without founder control.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Creators' constraint is execution, not ideation; without investor control, the deal structure provides insufficient downside protection.
bounded_by: Different assessment if deal structure reverses (investor 80%, creator 20%, investor-fronted capital)

claims.text: Investing in established creators (7-8 figure revenue) is effectively a joint venture requiring Hormozi to build a new business infrastructure, rather than a true investment; he would only pursue this if existing ACQ resources already contained the core competencies needed.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when considering later-stage creator company investment
claims.mechanism: Creator businesses bring distribution and image/likeness; if advisor lacks operational infrastructure to support, the investment becomes a business-building exercise, not a capital deployment.
bounded_by: Applies specifically when advisor does not already have operational systems; if infrastructure exists, evaluation changes

claims.text: When capital is deployed to a scaled business that already possesses the core competencies needed (e.g., operational expertise, team infrastructure), the capital deployment is lower-friction and higher-alpha than incubating a creator business from scratch.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when choosing between scaling existing business vs. incubating new venture
claims.mechanism: Deploying capital when core competencies are already present requires less total work and carries lower opportunity cost than building competencies from zero.
bounded_by: Assumes deal flow provides sufficient high-competency targets to justify not building

claims.text: The constraint for most creator businesses is not idea generation but execution and business acumen; therefore, investment in a creator is really an investment in systems and operational expertise, not in the creator's ideation capability.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when evaluating creator-founder fit for investment
claims.mechanism: Creators are typically selected for idea generation and content production; operational capability is the binding constraint at scale, not ideation.

examples.text: Hormozi describes his ACQ Ventures team: 'We have a lot of young, call it Bain, McKinsey consultants that will pull who are like, I hate feeling like a cog in a machine and just doing billable hours, but are otherwise incredibly hardworking, incredibly bright.' These hires wanted to see the problem-solving application beyond enterprise clients, and they came from his content world wanting to marry big business strategy with small business tactics.

Hormozi contrasts two investment structures with content creators: rejecting the traditional 'me owning 51%, investor owning 49%' model because it gives him insufficient control and high structural risk; considering instead 'maybe they owned 20% and we owned 80 and we fronted the capital and we put all the stuff together,' framing this as an incubation model.

When asked about investing in established creator companies ('like the Primes of the world...like a Logan Paul or Jake Paul'), Hormozi explains: 'Investing in someone like that isn't really investing. It's a joint venture...I'm starting another business.' He would only pursue it if his existing resources and assets already had 'a huge percentage of the core competencies required, not just in knowledge, in manpower.'

practices.text: When analyzing consulting value transfer, assess whether the problem-solving discipline (constraint-solving approach) transfers to your domain, rather than evaluating specific domain expertise.
If considering creator investment, evaluate deal structure first: does it provide sufficient control to absorb risk, or would it require you to build the entire operational infrastructure?

Before pursuing joint ventures or incubations, audit whether your existing resources already contain the core competencies needed; if building from zero is required, calculate opportunity cost against deal flow.
